textbookText: A spherical mirror is a mirror whose reflecting
surface is part of a sphere. A portion of a hollow glass
sphere taken out by cutting the sphere along a plane can serve as a spherical mirror if one surface is
silvered. Spherical mirrors are of two types; Concave
and convex. If the outer surface of portion APB of the sphere is
silvered as shown in figure 14.2(a) then, it behaves as a concave spherical mirror. On the other
hand, if the inner surface of the portion APB of the sphere is silvered as shown in figure 14.2(b)
then, it behaves as a convex spherical mirror.

The mirror formula is applicable for spherical mirrors (concave and convex) as well as plane mirrors.

Assumptions 1. The aperture of the mirror is small. 2. The incident and reflected rays make very small angles with the principal axis of the mirror. 3. The object is a point object situated on the principal axis.

Sign Conventions 1. The entire image distance and object distance are measured from the pole of the mirror. 2. The distances of real objects and real images are taken as positive, and those of virtual objects and virtual images are taken as negative. 3. The radius of curvature and focal length of a concave mirror are taken as positive, and those of convex are taken as negative.

14.5 Magnification "The ratio of the size of the image (I) formed by a mirror to the size of the object (O) is called image size (I) magnification of the mirror." Magnification of mirror (m) = object size (O) . . . (1)

The magnification of a mirror is also defined as the ratio of image distance (v) to object distance (u). image distance (v) The magnification of mirror, (m) = object distance (u) …(2) a) For the case of a real image, the magnification (m) is taken as positive.

b)For the case of a virtual image, the magnification (m) is taken as negative. c) If magnification is one, it will be of the same size as that of objects. d)If magnification is less than one, the image will be smaller in size in comparison to the size of the object. This is the case of diminished image. e) If magnification is more than one, the image will be larger in size in comparison to the size of the object. This is the case of an enlarged image. Magnification in mirrors indicates their ability to produce enlarged or reduced images. The production of enlarged or reduced images is very essential for us in many practical applications, scientific investigations, educational purposes and many more. For examples; a) Magnification produced by a concave mirror is used to determine the size and orientation of the image. b) Concave mirrors are used in various optical devices such as telescopes, microscopes, and make-up mirrors to get magnified images of small objects as well as distant objects. c) Convex mirrors produce virtual and diminished images so that they are used in vehicles for a wider field of rear view. d)Convex mirrors are commonly used in traffic mirrors, security mirrors, surveillance, etc. e) Magnified image helps to take precise and accurate readings during experiments.
Workout Examples: Q. Magnification of a plane mirror is always one, why?
A plane mirror can form an image of an object such that the size of the image is equal to the
size of the object. Magnification is the ratio of the size of the image to the size of the object.
